s: A company's interactive web application uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to serve images from an Amazon S3 bucket. Occasionally, third-party tools ingest corrupted images into the S3 bucket. This image corruption causes a poor user experience in the application later. The company has successfully implemented and tested Python logic to detect corrupt images. A solutions architect must recommend a solution to integrate the detection logic with minimal latency between the ingestion and serving. Which solution will meet these requirements?
o: Use a Lambda@Edge function that is invoked by a viewer-response event.
Use a Lambda@Edge function that is invoked by an origin-response event.
Use an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function.
Use an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Step Functions state machine.
e: This solution will allow the detection logic to be run as soon as the image is uploaded to the S3 bucket, before it is served to users via the CloudFront distribution. This way, the detection logic can quickly identify any corrupted images and prevent them from being served to users, minimizing latency between ingestion and serving. Reference: AWS Lambda@Edge documentation:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-edge.htmlYou can use Lambda@Edge to run your code in response to CloudFront events, such as a viewer request, an origin request, a response, or an error.
nt: Debated. Origin-response Lambda@Edge (the key) checks images as CloudFront fetches them. Many argue for an S3 event → Lambda (C), which checks at ingestion.

w.y: The aim is to catch corrupt images as soon as they arrive, before they are served. The key's origin-response Lambda@Edge checks images on cache misses so a corrupt image is never cached; the alternative (an S3 event-triggered Lambda) checks right after ingestion.

o.A: Wrong: viewer-response runs on every request, which adds latency each time and inspects content after it is cached.
o.B: Correct per the key: origin-response runs once per cache fill and can stop a corrupt image before CloudFront caches it.
o.C: Disputed: an S3 event plus Lambda checks each image right after upload with no added serving latency, but a corrupt image can be served before the check finishes.
o.D: Wrong: Step Functions adds overhead for a single detection step.

alt: C is a strong alternative: origin-response Lambda@Edge cannot read the response body, so to inspect the image it would have to fetch it again; an S3 event plus Lambda runs the Python check right after ingestion and adds no latency when serving. A second check found the Lambda@Edge answer weak: an origin-response function doesn't get the image body, so C (S3 event → Lambda validates each image at upload) is the stronger design.
